about: Formats and protocols that IRL streaming apps and services share, one entry per item. Each entry credits its maker; listing an item here does not mean this project makes, runs or endorses it. group: 'shared' when several makers' products write or read it; 'app-formats' for one app's own format that a named second product also writes or reads; 'hardware-codecs' for the video and audio codecs and the camera interfaces (UVC, HDMI, SDI) a stream goes through; 'steward-projects' for items made by people who steward this repository, kept apart so they are not mistaken for established standards. An entry that is also a glossary word shares its words.json id, sets word to it and carries no description of its own. Codecs carry codec facts and transports carry transport facts (licensing, efficiency, hardware support, bonding, latency, loss recovery, platform ingest); each fact has its own sources and checked_on, and unverified: true marks a claim the makers' or platforms' own pages don't confirm. service_ids link products in services.json; other_users names products that are not catalogued. Descriptions are our own words; sources are public primary pages. checked_on is the day the entry was compared with its sources.

standards.name: SRT (Secure Reliable Transport)
standards.notes: Support in each listed product follows its services.json entry.

bonding.text: Built in: libsrt socket groups send over several links at once (broadcast) or switch to a backup; balancing is still under development.

latency.text: A receive buffer you set (latency, 120 ms by default) that decides how long missing packets may take.

loss_recovery.text: Resends lost packets (ARQ); forward error correction (FEC) can be added.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

youtube.text: Not listed; YouTube takes RTMP/RTMPS and HLS.

sources.label: YouTube Help: set up an HLS stream

kick.text: Not listed; Kick's help gives an RTMPS address.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: srt:// and srtla:// stream URLs
standards.maker: Haivision (srt://); srtla:// has no single maker
standards.description: One line that holds the host, port, stream ID and options such as latency, which a relay hands out and an app pastes in.
standards.notes: srtla:// borrows the srt:// shape, but no maker publishes its rules, and apps differ on which query options they accept.

standards.name: SRT Stream ID
standards.maker: Haivision (recommended syntax); each receiver sets its own keys
standards.description: The text field that tells a receiver which stream you are publishing or playing.
standards.notes: The field is shared; the convention is not. Haivision recommends an optional '#!::' key=value syntax, while IRL receivers use their own keys (SRT Live Server style 'uplive.sls/live/<name>', OpenIRL 'live_<key>' and 'play_<key>').

standards.name: SRTLA (SRT link aggregation)
standards.notes: The reference code and its README describe it; there is no separate spec. srtla2 is incompatible with earlier srtla. BELABOX marks its own receiver (srtla_rec) unsupported and points to BELABOX Cloud; the other receivers are independent implementations. Sender support follows the services.json entries.

bonding.text: It is the bonding: one SRT stream spread over several links, balanced by how each link is doing.

latency.text: SRT's buffer you set; it also covers packets arriving out of order from different links.

loss_recovery.text: SRT's own resends, which srtla also uses to balance the links.

licensing.text: AGPL-3.0 reference code from BELABOX; no separate spec.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

youtube.text: Not listed; YouTube takes RTMP/RTMPS and HLS.

sources.label: YouTube Help: set up an HLS stream

kick.text: Not listed; Kick's help gives an RTMPS address.

standards.name: Moblink
standards.description: Lets spare phones, or a router, lend their own mobile data to the streaming phone as extra bonding connections.
standards.notes: No written spec; the MIT code is the reference. IRL+ Cast support follows its services.json entry.

bonding.text: Add-on: spare phones become extra SRTLA bonding links.

latency.text: The SRT buffer of the stream it carries.

loss_recovery.text: The SRT resends of the stream it carries.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

standards.name: RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport)
standards.maker: Video Services Forum (RIST Activity Group); librist by VideoLAN
standards.description: A broadcast-industry alternative to SRT for sending video over the internet, with its own multi-link bonding.
standards.notes: Support in the other listed products follows their services.json entries.

bonding.text: Built in: the Main Profile supports several links, load-balanced or redundant (librist).

latency.text: A receive buffer you set, from 50 ms to 30 seconds in librist.

licensing.text: VSF TR-06 specifications; librist under BSD-2-Clause.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

standards.name: NDI (Network Device Interface)
standards.description: Video between cameras, computers and apps on the same network, with very little delay; some cameras send it directly.
standards.notes: OBS speaks NDI through the DistroAV plugin. NDI|HX cameras send compressed NDI from the camera itself.

bonding.text: No bonding of internet links; NDI 4's multipath TCP spreads one stream over several network cards.

latency.text: Real-time: NDI's docs describe Reliable UDP as low latency, with minimal delay.

loss_recovery.text: Reliable UDP (the NDI 5 default) asks for lost packets again; a UDP mode with FEC also exists.

licensing.text: Proprietary SDK from Vizrt NDI AB, offered under NDI's own terms.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

youtube.text: Not listed; YouTube takes RTMP/RTMPS and HLS.

standards.name: WHIP (WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol)
standards.description: A standard way to send a WebRTC (very low latency) stream to a server with one HTTP request.
standards.notes: RFC 9725, a Proposed Standard published in March 2025.

bonding.text: No; RFC 9725 sets up one WebRTC session.

latency.text: Real-time by design: WebRTC aims for the lowest possible latency.

twitch.text: Not listed; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, whose Twitch servers are all rtmp:// addresses.

youtube.text: Not listed; YouTube takes RTMP/RTMPS and HLS.

sources.label: YouTube Help: set up an HLS stream

kick.text: Not listed; Kick's help gives an RTMPS address.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: WHEP (WebRTC-HTTP Egress Protocol)
standards.description: The playback side of WHIP: watch a WebRTC stream with one HTTP request, for example as a low-latency preview.
standards.notes: An Internet-Draft (draft-05, October 2026) in IESG evaluation; not an RFC yet.

standards.name: Enhanced RTMP (E-RTMP)
standards.description: Brings modern codecs (HEVC, AV1, Opus), multitrack and reconnect to the old RTMP protocol.
standards.notes: The adopters follow Veovera's own adoption list, not a test of each product.

bonding.text: No; RTMP runs over a single TCP connection.

latency.text: No buffer to set; it rides on TCP, which waits for its own resends.

loss_recovery.text: TCP resends lost data; E-RTMP adds a reconnect request from the server.

licensing.text: Open spec under Apache-2.0 from Veovera.

twitch.text: Plain RTMP, yes (Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json). Veovera lists Twitch as an adopter, through Enhanced Broadcasting.

youtube.text: Yes: RTMP/RTMPS, with HEVC and AV1 as well as H.264.

kick.text: RTMPS with H.264 only, so plain RTMP but none of the newer codecs.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: OBS WebSocket (v5)
standards.description: The remote-control line into OBS: switch scenes, start and stop, read status. It never carries the video.
standards.notes: Built into OBS Studio since version 28. Client support follows the services.json entries.

standards.name: Receiver stats endpoints
standards.maker: Each receiver's maker; NOALBS maintains the parsers
standards.description: The web address a receiver offers with live bitrate, round-trip time and lost packets, which scene switchers and overlays read.
standards.notes: Not one format but one shape per server: NOALBS keeps 14 parser modules, the nearest thing to a shared reference. Some receivers reuse another's shape; irl-srt-server keeps SRT Live Server's.

standards.name: BELABOX Cloud remote
standards.description: The WebSocket through BELABOX Cloud that lets a bot, switcher or dashboard see and control a BELABOX from anywhere.
standards.notes: BELABOX runs the service; the other tools connect to it. There is no published protocol description, so clients follow belaUI's code.

standards.name: RealtimeIRL location API
standards.licence: MIT (@rtirl/api client); the service is closed
standards.description: A phone pushes its location to rtirl.com with a push key; map and speed overlays read it with a pull key.
standards.notes: The pull side and the client library are documented; the push call appears only in the apps' code.

standards.name: DJI camera Bluetooth control
standards.description: Bluetooth commands to an Osmo camera, which IRL apps use to start the camera's own RTMP live stream.
standards.notes: DJI documents the protocol for recording, modes and GPS. The live-stream setup is Moblin's own work, which dji-remote ported; the video itself is plain RTMP. The licence of DJI's demo repository is unclear.

standards.name: Moblin settings link (moblin://)
standards.description: A link or QR code that adds a stream (URL, codec, OBS remote and more) to Moblin in one tap.
standards.notes: Other makers write it (IRLhosting, IAR1) and another app (Brix) reads it.

standards.name: Moblin settings export
standards.description: Moblin's full backup of streams, scenes, widgets and presets, which another tool can read to check a setup.
standards.notes: Moblin's internal settings JSON; it can change with any release. Scenes, widgets and presets live inside it, with no separate format of their own.

standards.name: Larix Grove (larix://set/v1)
standards.description: A link or QR code that loads connections and encoder settings into Larix Broadcaster, and also into IRL Pro.
standards.notes: IRL Pro reading it is stated by IRLhosting and IRLToolkit, not on IRL Pro's own pages.

standards.name: IRLwhatever import link
standards.description: An irlwhatever://import/ link carrying a stream's name, URL and SRT latency.
standards.notes: No description from the maker was found; IRLhosting documents what its links carry.

standards.name: NOALBS config.json
standards.description: The scene switcher's settings file: which stats to read, which scenes to switch to, which chat to answer.
standards.notes: IRLhosting's config generator writes it and its config checker reads it.

standards.name: H.264 / AVC
standards.maker: ITU-T and ISO/IEC MPEG (Joint Video Team)
standards.description: The video codec every streaming app, box and platform handles; the safe default.
standards.notes: Also called AVC or MPEG-4 Part 10. Support in the listed products follows their services.json entries and READMEs.

licensing.text: Patent pool run by Via LA. Its page says royalties are spread across the value chain, with thresholds below which some aren't charged.

ios.text: Apple's own docs read here name HEVC, not H.264; iPhones still record and stream H.264.

sources.label: Apple Support: HEIF and HEVC on Apple devices

android.text: Android lists an H.264 encoder (Main profile from Android 6) and decoder. Whether it runs in hardware depends on the phone.

rk3588.text: Encode up to 8K at 30 fps, decode up to 8K at 60 fps.

intel.text: Decode and encode from Broadwell (5th gen Core) in Intel's media driver.

nvidia.text: NVENC and NVDEC from the first Maxwell GPUs.

sources.label: NVIDIA video encode and decode support matrix

apple_mac.text: Apple's media engine accelerates H.264 (stated for M3 chips).

twitch.text: Yes. Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, which lists H.264 for Twitch.

sources.label: YouTube Help: set up an HLS stream

kick.text: Yes; Kick says it supports only H.264 (x264).

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: HEVC / H.265
standards.description: The successor to H.264: a sharper picture at the same bitrate, which helps on weak mobile links.
standards.notes: Support in the listed products follows their services.json entries and makers' pages.

licensing.text: Patent pools run by Access Advance (HEVC Advance) and Via LA (HEVC/VVC). Via LA's licence covers devices; Access Advance lists devices, software and content on physical media.

efficiency.text: About half the bitrate of H.264 for the same picture, says ITU-T (2013).

ios.text: iPhone 7 and later record HEVC, says Apple; older devices play it with limits.

sources.label: Apple Support: HEIF and HEVC on Apple devices

android.text: Android lists an HEVC decoder from Android 5 but no platform encoder; encoding depends on the phone.

rk3588.text: Encode up to 8K at 30 fps, decode up to 8K at 60 fps.

intel.text: Decode and encode from Skylake (6th gen Core) in Intel's media driver.

nvidia.text: Encode from Pascal GPUs, decode from second-generation Maxwell.

sources.label: NVIDIA video encode and decode support matrix

apple_mac.text: Apple's media engine accelerates HEVC (stated for M3 chips).

twitch.text: Not for a normal stream: Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, which lists only H.264. Twitch said in 2024 its Enhanced Broadcasting beta was experimenting with HEVC.

sources.label: Twitch blog: Enhanced Broadcasting beta (8 Jan 2024)

youtube.text: Yes, over RTMP/RTMPS and HLS; HDR needs HEVC.

sources.label: YouTube Help: set up an HLS stream

kick.text: No; Kick says it doesn't support H.265.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick
Kick Help: OBS or Streamlabs not connecting

standards.name: AV1
standards.description: An open, royalty-free video codec from AOMedia, newer than HEVC; hardware encoders are still rare on IRL gear.
standards.notes: OBS and FFmpeg follow Veovera's Enhanced RTMP adoption list, which carries AV1 over RTMP.

licensing.text: AOMedia members license their AV1 patents royalty-free (AOMedia Patent License 1.0). Sisvel separately runs a royalty-bearing AV1 pool for consumer products.

efficiency.text: 50.3% fewer bits than x264 main profile and 46.2% fewer than x264 high profile at the same quality (BD-rate), in Facebook's 2018 test of 400 videos.

ios.text: A17 Pro (iPhone 15 Pro) and later have an AV1 decoder; Apple names no AV1 encoder.

android.text: Android 14 makes an AV1 encoder and decoder mandatory; they may run in software.

rk3588.text: Decodes AV1 up to 8K at 60 fps; Rockchip lists only H.264 and H.265 encoders.

intel.text: Decode from Tiger Lake (11th gen Core); encode on Arc (DG2) and Meteor Lake and later.

nvidia.text: Decode from Ampere (RTX 30); encode from Ada Lovelace (RTX 40).

sources.label: NVIDIA video encode and decode support matrix

apple_mac.text: M3 chips and later decode AV1; Apple names no AV1 encoder.

twitch.text: Not for a normal stream: Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, which lists only H.264. Twitch said in 2024 its Enhanced Broadcasting beta was experimenting with AV1.

sources.label: Twitch blog: Enhanced Broadcasting beta (8 Jan 2024)

youtube.text: Yes, over RTMP/RTMPS; not for HDR.

kick.text: No; Kick says it supports only H.264.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: AAC (Advanced Audio Coding)
standards.description: The usual audio codec for RTMP streams and most platforms.
standards.notes: Part of MPEG-4 Audio (ISO/IEC 14496-3). Android phones encode AAC-LC as part of the platform.

licensing.text: Via LA licenses AAC patents to makers of encoder and decoder products. It says no fees are due for broadcasting or streaming AAC.

twitch.text: Most likely yes; Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, which names no audio codec for Twitch.

youtube.text: Yes; YouTube asks for AAC or MP3, and 5.1 sound only with AAC over RTMP/RTMPS.

kick.text: Kick's help asks for stereo at up to 48 kHz but names no audio codec.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: Opus
standards.description: An open, royalty-free audio codec, used by WebRTC (WHIP) and Enhanced RTMP.
standards.notes: Every WebRTC endpoint, and so every WHIP sender and receiver, must support Opus (RFC 7874). OBS and FFmpeg follow Veovera's Enhanced RTMP adoption list.

licensing.text: Royalty-free patent licences from Xiph.Org, Broadcom and Microsoft; BSD-licensed code in RFC 6716. Some other companies have disclosed patents with possibly royalty-bearing terms, the Opus site says.

efficiency.text: Rated above HE-AAC at 64 kb/s and above LC-AAC at 96 kb/s in HydrogenAudio's public listening tests on stereo music, linked from opus-codec.org.

twitch.text: Twitch's help pages need JavaScript; this follows OBS's services.json, which names no audio codec for Twitch.

youtube.text: Not listed; YouTube asks for AAC or MP3.

kick.text: Kick's help names no audio codec.

sources.label: Kick Help: how to stream on Kick

standards.name: UVC (USB Video Class)
standards.description: The standard way a USB camera or HDMI capture stick shows up as a camera, with no driver to install.

sources.label: USB-IF: Video Class v1.5 document set

standards.notes: Moblin supports UVC cameras on iPad; support in the Android apps and the mixer follows their services.json entries.

standards.name: HDMI
standards.licence: Licensed to adopters by HDMI LA, with adopter and licensing fees
standards.maker: HDMI Forum; licensed by HDMI Licensing Administrator (HDMI LA)
standards.description: The camera's video-out cable; IRL boxes take it in directly or through a USB capture stick.
standards.notes: The specification is available to adopters; HDMI LA's public page names adopter and licensing fees but no amounts.

standards.name: SDI (Serial Digital Interface)
standards.licence: SMPTE standards (ST 259, ST 292 and later), freely accessible from SMPTE
standards.description: The locking broadcast video cable on pro cameras; some bonded encoders take it in.
standards.notes: SMPTE says its standards library is freely accessible; HD-SDI and 3G/12G-SDI are later versions.

standards.name: stream-status
standards.description: A JSON format for live-stream findings: what's wrong, where, how sure, and whether the stream is still live.
standards.notes: A v0 draft; field names can still change. No app writes or reads it yet.

standards.name: stream-session
standards.description: A proposed format from openstreambox that has not been published yet.
standards.notes: Nothing public to check yet; this entry gains a link and sources once it is published.

standards.name: irl-commons
standards.description: This catalogue: small curated datasets about IRL streaming, with Zod and JSON Schema validation.
standards.notes: A v0 catalogue. No outside users are named yet, and the npm package is not published.
